title: Informal Question (correct exponential constant in r(n,m))
statement_text: Is $3$, the lower bound on $r(n,m)$ given by considering a random set, the right exponential constant? That is, does $r(n,m) = N^{1-\varepsilon_m}$ hold with the same exponential base $3$ as in the random lower bound $r(n,m) \geq N^{1-(m+1)3^{-m}}$, rather than the base $C \approx 13.901$ appearing in the upper bound $r(n,m) \leq (1+o(1))N^{1-C^{-m}}$?
context_text: $r(n,m)$ is the maximum size of a subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ containing no affine $m$-dimensional subspace (the multidimensional cap set problem), and $N=3^n$. A random set gives $r(n,m)\ge N^{1-(m+1)3^{-m}}$. In the other direction, the arithmetic triangle removal lemma of Fox and Lovász implies that every subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ of density $\alpha$ has three-term arithmetic progression density at least $\alpha^C$ with $C\approx13.901$; choosing the most popular nonzero common difference $d$ and inducting on $m$ gives $r(n,m)\le(1+o(1))N^{1-C^{-m}}$. Both bounds have the form $N^{1-\varepsilon_m}$ with $\varepsilon_m\to0$ exponentially fast in $m$, but with exponential base $3$ versus $C$; the authors ask whether the right base is $3$, $C$, or something in between. For a prime $p$, $\alpha>0$ and $\beta<\alpha^3$, $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ is the least positive integer such that for every $n\ge n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ and every $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of density at least $\alpha$, there is a nonzero $d\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$ such that the density of three-term arithmetic progressions $x,x+d,x+2d$ (over $x$) lying in $A$ is at least $\beta$; it exists by a theorem of Green (popular differences), and fails to exist for $\beta\ge\alpha^3$. If $n\ge n_3(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\beta=\alpha^{3+o(1)}$, the same induction would show that $3$ is the correct base; but the authors determine, for $p\ge19$, the tower height of $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ up to constant factors, and it grows for $\beta=\alpha^{3+o(1)}$, giving strong evidence that this popular-differences approach cannot settle the question. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.

title: Conjecture (Theorem 2 extends to primes p < 19)
statement_text: The following bounds on the tower height of $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$, proved for primes $p\ge19$, should also hold for all primes $p<19$: for $0<\alpha\le1/2$, $\alpha^3>\beta>\alpha^{3+e^{-133}}$ and $\epsilon=\alpha^3-\beta$, (i) if $\epsilon<\alpha^3/(\log(1/\alpha))^{\log p}$, then $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ grows as a tower of $p$'s of height $\Theta(\log(\alpha^3/\epsilon))\pm O_p(1)$; (ii) if $\alpha^3/(\log(1/\alpha))^{\log p}\le\epsilon<\alpha^3(1-2^{-8-8C_p})$, it grows as a tower of $p$'s of height $\Theta((\log p)\log\log(1/\alpha))\pm O_p(1)$; (iii) otherwise it grows as a tower of $p$'s of height $\Theta\big((\log p)\log\frac{\log(1/\alpha)}{\log(\alpha^3/\beta)}\big)\pm O_p(1)$ with a $1/\beta$ on top.
context_text: For a prime $p$, $\alpha>0$ and $\beta<\alpha^3$, $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ is the least positive integer such that for every $n\ge n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ and every $A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$ of density at least $\alpha$, there is a nonzero $d\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$ such that the density of three-term arithmetic progressions $x,x+d,x+2d$ (over $x$) lying in $A$ is at least $\beta$; it exists by a theorem of Green (popular differences), and fails to exist for $\beta\ge\alpha^3$. $C_p=\Theta(\log p)$ is the exponent in the arithmetic triangle removal lemma in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ (every set of density $\alpha$ has three-term progression density at least $\alpha^{C_p}$), and $\pm O_p(1)$ means up to an additive error depending only on $p$. For $\beta$ much smaller (below $\alpha^{3+e^{-133}}$) the growth of $n_p(\alpha,\beta)$ is a tower of constant height with $\log(1/\alpha)$ on top, and for $\alpha$ close to $1$ the behaviour is different and determined separately. The authors prove the three-case result for $p\ge19$ (for instance, half the random bound, $\beta=\alpha^3/2$, requires a tower of height $\Theta((\log p)\log\log(1/\alpha))$) and conjecture it for $p<19$. The upper bounds hold for all primes, as does the lower bound when $\epsilon$ is small; only the case of large $\epsilon$ is missing, because the lower-bound construction uses bounds on the largest subset of $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ without a three-term progression, and the known bounds are not good enough for small $p$. This is additive combinatorics rather than graph theory.
